cells.tense: The pen is in your hand and the aim is already written.
cells.act: hold your shape under the weight
cells.ask: Name where you're headed in words you'd use. Then take the next step of it today, in the way you already work, and keep your shape while you do.
cells.core:
You can point energy at a chosen aim and keep it pointed. The direction is yours, and it rests on something you could name if someone asked, which is the difference between heading somewhere and being carried. What goes well here is plain: the end doesn't move when a week goes badly, because you are walking it, not being pushed.
There is a cheap way to test it. Put the aim into words you'd actually use, then do one piece of it today the way you do things. The road doesn't need the speech; it needs the walking. What you keep afterward is the fact that you chose the step you took, and the shape you kept while taking it — the aim holding you as much as you holding it.
cells.sheetLine: You can say where you're going and keep going there.
cells.verb: choosing the direction and holding it
cells.place: the stretch of road you are already walking and won't leave

cells.tense: The future is being braced against before it has arrived in the room.
cells.act: see the whole pattern you are standing inside
cells.ask: Stop steering for a moment and look at the whole shape around you — the aim, the roads, the people on them. Draw it if a page helps, and mark where you stand.
cells.core:
Where the aim is real, the grip has tightened past the point of steering. You are pushing on tomorrow already, settling things that haven't happened, and the push looks like commitment from the inside. It isn't force of will; it's will spent on a future you can't touch, and the toll comes out of today. The pace is running ahead of anything the road can meet.
One honest look at the layout covers more ground than a week of bracing. Stand where you can see the arrangement — the aim, the roads you keep refusing, the people already on them — and put yourself somewhere on that picture. Seeing it doesn't have to finish. You can know it more deeply than last time, and the push can rest for a minute while you look.

cells.tense: The aim ran down and nothing in you points anywhere now.
cells.act: let what you are show without dimming it
cells.ask: Choose something today and do it your own way, with nobody told why. No reason, no use, no explaining. Do it, then carry on with your day.
cells.core:
The energy that used to point somewhere has stopped, and the stop has gone on long enough to feel like the shape of the world. You are not lazy. The aim ran down after enough resistance, and what's left is waiting with nothing pointed at it. The direction itself is still true; it didn't need that last road.
The way back opens from the side, not the front. Choose a piece of today and do it in your own way — no reason, no use, nothing said about it — and let what you are show through your hands without defending any of it. Don't try to feel direction while you do. Do the thing. The charge comes from underneath, the way it did before, and effort aimed straight at it will only persuade you it's gone.

cells.tense: The pen is down in a room you are already writing in.
cells.act: put your own name on what is already yours
cells.ask: Look at what you are already in the middle of and say, plainly, that you picked it. If it was picked for you, say that instead. Leave the rest alone for now.
cells.core:
Your direction keeps moving, and the moment of choosing has slipped out of view. You keep pace with something — a routine, a promise to people, an old ambition — and the pace is steady, so it passes for a decision. It isn't that the aim is wrong. You have stopped marking which part of it you picked, and the day fills with movement that doesn't ask who is doing it.
One honest naming puts the pen back. Look at what you are already in the middle of and state plainly that you chose it — or that it was chosen for you; either one tells the truth. Then leave the rest alone and keep walking. Naming isn't management. It puts your own name on what is already yours, so the next mile is walked by you and not only by the pace you kept.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person's current direction is consciously chosen; Balanced says the pen is in hand, but the record cannot show that from outside. A reasonable reader could say the aims were inherited or the momentum never stopped, and at Balanced the ask still teaches something the person can use if the read is wrong — it names a direction in their own words and acts on it, which works whether or not they wrote it. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any line about the pen being theirs; read the drafts as if the person never picked the pen up.
